title: Poll Shows Majority of Voters See 2026 Midterms as Trump‑Centric and Disapprove】
body:
A fresh poll released this week shows that the looming 2026 congressional midterms have become, in the eyes of most American voters, a referendum on former President Donald Trump. By a margin of 12 points, registered voters say they would rather see Democrats control the House and Senate than Republicans, a shift that analysts attribute largely to Trump’s lingering unpopularity and the perception that the GOP’s agenda is still tethered to his legacy.

The NPR/PBS News/Marist survey, which interviewed more than 2,000 registered voters across the political spectrum, found that 58 % of respondents said they wanted a Democratic Congress, while only 46 % expressed a preference for a Republican one. The margin widened among independents, with 61 % favoring Democrats versus 38 % for Republicans. Notably, the poll revealed that 71 % of voters who identify as “strongly opposed” to Trump also said they would support Democratic candidates, whereas just 22 % of “strong Trump supporters” indicated a desire for a Democratic sweep. The data suggests that Trump’s personal brand continues to dominate the national conversation, even as he remains out of office.

Political strategists say the findings underscore a broader trend that has been building since the 2022 midterms: the Republican Party’s struggle to distance itself from Trump’s polarizing style while still courting his base. “Voters are not just reacting to policy proposals; they’re reacting to the personality that defines the party,” said Dr. Elena Ramirez, a professor of political science at Georgetown University. “When a former president remains such a focal point, it creates a liability for any candidate who cannot convincingly separate themselves from that narrative.” The poll’s respondents echoed this sentiment, with 64 % saying that the presence of Trump in the political discourse makes them more likely to vote Democratic, even if they are not traditionally aligned with the party.

The survey also highlighted specific issues that are shaping voter attitudes. Among those who cited Trump as a decisive factor, the most common concerns were the economy (57 %), immigration (49 %) and the perceived erosion of democratic norms (45 %). Conversely, Democratic-leaning respondents pointed to health care affordability (62 %) and climate action (58 %) as top priorities. These issue-based differences suggest that while Trump’s personal brand is a powerful motivator, policy considerations remain pivotal in shaping the electorate’s choices.

Republican leaders are already grappling with the implications of the poll. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell warned that the party must “recalibrate its messaging” to avoid being reduced to a single‑issue campaign centered on Trump. In a closed‑door meeting with GOP governors, the party’s strategy team reportedly debated whether to elevate younger, less‑Trump‑aligned candidates in swing districts. Some state parties have begun to promote “future‑focused” platforms that emphasize infrastructure, technology, and education, hoping to broaden appeal beyond the former president’s base.

Democratic officials, meanwhile, are interpreting the data as validation of their effort to frame the 2026 contest as a battle for the nation’s democratic health. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the poll “confirms that voters are tired of the chaos and division that have come to define the Republican brand under Trump’s influence.” The party’s national committee has already begun allocating additional resources to competitive races in the Midwest and South, where the Trump effect appears strongest.

Looking ahead, the poll suggests that the 2026 midterms could produce a decisive Democratic advantage, provided the party can sustain momentum and translate voter sentiment into turnout. However, political landscapes can shift rapidly; economic downturns, foreign crises, or a resurgence of Trump’s political activity could reshape the calculus. For now, the data paints a picture of an electorate eager to move beyond the Trump era, a sentiment that may well shape the strategies and outcomes of the next round of congressional battles.
